![](../../src/images/hex_complex.png){.intro_image}

The fundamental data object in R is the **atomic vector**. Atomic vectors form the building block of every other data object that we will use in this course, and in fact any *single* number or word in R is itself an atomic vector of length one. An atomic vector has a **type**, which tells us what kind of values it contains. All values within a single atomic vector must share the same type. An atomic vector can also have a **class**, which affects how R treats the object and may differ from its underlying type.

In this lesson, we will explore four kinds of vectors that you will encounter often in this course: numeric vectors (including the double and integer types), character vectors, factors, and logical vectors. You will learn:

* The difference between double numeric and integer vectors
* How to work with character values, including when single quotes are (and are not) necessary
* What a factor is and why the order of its levels matters
* How logical values are represented and tested, including a common mistake that catches almost everyone at least once

[{{< fa exclamation-triangle size=2x >}} Important!]{style="color: red;"} This lesson assumes that you have completed [Preliminary Lesson 2: Environment & Functions](https://evansbrians.github.io/gis_2026/module_0/0.2_environment_and_functions/){target="_blank"}. The material here builds on that lesson, so please complete it before moving on.

</div>

## Before you begin

To get the most out of this lesson, please:

* Open RStudio in a clean session.
* Open a new, blank script file and save it as "lesson_0.3.R".
* Code along with the content.

## Numbers

R represents the numbers that we will use in this course with two types:

* **Double**: R's default numeric type, which can represent values with or without a fractional portion.
* **Integer**: A whole number stored with integer type.

Let's create an atomic vector of numbers and assign it to the name `number_object`:

```{r}
number_object <-
  c(1, 1, 2, 3)

number_object
```

We can determine the class of the vector with the `class()` function:

```{r}
class(number_object)
```

How an atomic vector is stored in your computer is known as its **type**. We use `typeof()` to determine this:

```{r}
typeof(number_object)
```

Notice that the vector's class is `"numeric"`, while its type is `"double"`. Unsuffixed numeric values such as `1`, `2`, and `3` are doubles by default -- even when they are whole numbers!

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: Unsuffixed whole-number values, such as those in `c(1, 1, 2, 3)`, have integer type because they are whole numbers.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(FALSE)`
:::

To generate an integer vector of adjacent whole numbers, we use the colon function (`:`), which generates a regular sequence from a starting to an ending value:

```{r}
my_integers <- 1:3

class(my_integers)

typeof(my_integers)
```

If we want to generate an integer vector with `c()`, we add an uppercase `L` after each value:

```{r}
class(
  c(1L, 1L, 2L, 3L)
)
```

We can also convert a double numeric vector to an integer vector with `as.integer()`:

```{r}
class(
  as.integer(
    c(1, 1, 2, 3)
  )
)
```

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [`as.integer()` truncates, it does not round!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

If you need to preserve the numeric values exactly, only use `as.integer()` when the values are already whole numbers. Otherwise, the conversion changes the values because `as.integer()` truncates rather than rounds. Notice what happens when we convert values with fractional portions to integers:

```{r}
as.integer(
  c(1.1, 2.3, 5.8)
)
```

`as.integer()` truncated (i.e., dropped) the decimal portion of each value rather than rounding to the nearest whole number.
:::

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: `as.integer(c(1.1, 2.3, 5.8))` rounds each value to the nearest whole number.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(FALSE)`
:::

Likewise, we use `as.numeric()` to convert an integer vector to a double numeric vector:

```{r}
class(
  as.numeric(1:3)
)

typeof(
  as.numeric(1:3)
)
```

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Test your knowledge!]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

1. Which of the following produces an atomic vector whose type is integer?

`r longmcq(c("c(1, 2, 3)", answer = "1:3", "c(1.0, 2.0, 3.0)", "as.numeric(1:3)"))`

## Characters

A **character vector** stores text strings, which may include letters, numbers, spaces, and punctuation.

When you enter a character value directly in R code, enclose it in quotation marks. The code below creates a character vector and assigns it to the name `months`:

```{r}
months <-
  c(
    "March",
    "February",
    "January",
    "January"
  )
```

The class and type of a character vector are both `"character"`:

```{r}
class(months)

typeof(months)
```

Any atomic vector can be converted to a character vector with `as.character()`:

```{r}
as.character(1:5)
```

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Which function converts an atomic vector of any class into a character vector?]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r longmcq(c(answer = "as.character()", "as.numeric()", "typeof()", "c()"))`
:::

### Single or double quotes?

Single (`'hello world'`) and double (`"hello world"`) quotes can largely be used interchangeably in R. **In this course, we will always use double quotes for character values** -- this is the convention set out in our [Course style guide](https://evansbrians.github.io/gis_2026/resources/course_style_guide/){target="_blank"} and it matches the [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#character-vectors){target="_blank"}.

The main situation in which you will need to reach for single quotes is when the character value itself contains a double quote. Watch what happens when we try to enclose a quoted phrase in double quotes:

```{r}
#| error: true

"Maude said, "to me they will always be glorious birds""
```

R reads the second double quote as the *end* of the string, and has no idea what to do with the text that follows. We can resolve this by enclosing the entire value in single quotes instead:

```{r}
'Maude said, "to me they will always be glorious birds"'
```

The reverse problem occurs if a character value contains an apostrophe and is enclosed in single quotes:

```{r}
#| error: true

'Maude's Cadillac'
```

Because our course convention is to default to double quotes, this particular problem should rarely come up -- but it is worth knowing that the fix is the same in either direction (switch to the other kind of quote) or that you can **escape** the problematic character with a backslash, which tells R to treat the following character literally:

```{r}
"Maude's Cadillac"

'Maude said, "to me they will always be glorious birds"'

"Maude said, \"to me they will always be glorious birds\""
```

::: mysecret
{{< fa screwdriver-wrench size=2x >}} [So when *should* I use single quotes?]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

In this course, use single quotes only when the character value contains a double quote and you choose not to escape that quote. Otherwise, use double quotes -- this is one of the rules that our automated style checks will flag!
:::

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Test your knowledge!]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

1. You need a character value that itself contains a double quote. Which approach works?

`r longmcq(c(answer = "Enclose the whole value in single quotes, or escape the inner double quote with a backslash", "There is no way to include a double quote in a string", "Type two double quotes in a row", "Remove the inner quote -- R does not allow it"))`

2. True or false: in this course, single and double quotes should be used interchangeably, based on whichever you happen to type first.

`r torf(FALSE)`
:::

## Factors

A **factor** is a vector that represents categorical values using integer codes and character levels. A factor contains two pieces of information:

* **Integer values**: An integer code associated with each value.
* **Levels**: The character values associated with each integer code.

*Note: The `factor()` function also has a **labels** argument, which we will use below. Supplying `labels` renames the categories as the factor is created -- the new names are then stored as the factor's levels.*

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [A factor stores two pieces of information. Which pair correctly names them?]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r longmcq(c("Class and dimension", answer = "Integer values and levels", "Names and attributes", "Rows and columns"))`
:::

Factors are useful when a variable takes one of a limited set of categories (e.g., "juvenile" and "adult"), especially when you care about the order in which those categories are displayed (e.g., "small", "medium", "large").

We create a factor with the `factor()` function, supplying a character vector as the first argument:

```{r}
example_factor <-
  factor(
    c(
      "one",
      "one",
      "two",
      "three"
    )
  )

class(example_factor)

typeof(example_factor)
```

Notice that the type is `"integer"` even though we typed in words!

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: A factor is stored in your computer as an integer type, even though you create it by supplying a character vector to `factor()`.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(TRUE)`
:::

Let's have a look at the object itself:

```{r}
example_factor
```

There are four values, but they have been grouped into three levels. We can see the integer codes mapped to each level with `as.integer()`:

```{r}
as.integer(example_factor)
```

::: mysecret
{{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Factor levels are sorted by default!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

Notice that "one" was assigned the integer 1, "three" was assigned 2, and "two" was assigned 3. By default, factor levels are sorted -- usually alphabetically according to the current locale -- rather than ordered by their first appearance in the data. This can cause real problems when a factor's levels have a natural, non-alphabetical order (e.g., "low", "medium", "high").
:::

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: When you create a factor with `factor()` without specifying levels, the levels are ordered according to the order in which the values first appear in the data.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(FALSE)`
:::

We can plot a factor to see the count of values at each level:

```{r}
plot(example_factor)
```

Given the x-axis labels, this order doesn't make a lot of sense. We can manually set the level order with the `levels` argument:

```{r}
plot(
  factor(
    c("one", "one", "two", "three"),
    levels = c("one", "two", "three")
  )
)
```

## Logical values

R reserves the words `TRUE` and `FALSE` as **logical constants**. Their type is `"logical"`. When a numeric operation requires numbers, R coerces `FALSE` to 0 and `TRUE` to 1, which means we can evaluate them numerically:

```{r}
FALSE + TRUE

mean(
  c(FALSE, TRUE)
)
```

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: `TRUE` and `FALSE` have logical type, but a numeric operation coerces them to 1 and 0, so `FALSE + TRUE` evaluates to 1.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(TRUE)`
:::

### Logical operators

We generate logical values by testing an object with a **logical operator**:

| Operator | Usage      | Meaning                                    |
|:--------:|:----------:|:-------------------------------------------|
| `==`     | `x == y`   | x is equal to y                            |
| `!=`     | `x != y`   | x is NOT equal to y                        |
| `!`      | `!(x)`     | NOT x                                      |
| `\|`     | `x \| y`   | x OR y                                     |
| `&`      | `x & y`    | x AND y                                    |
| `%in%`   | `x %in% y` | each value of x is found within y          |
| `<`      | `x < y`    | x is less than y                           |
| `<=`     | `x <= y`   | x is less than or equal to y               |
| `>`      | `x > y`    | x is greater than y                        |
| `>=`     | `x >= y`   | x is greater than or equal to y            |

```{r}
3 < 4

3 > 4

2:4 == 3
```

::: mysecret
{{< fa screwdriver-wrench size=2x >}} [Be careful when comparing two sets of values with `==`!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"}

This is one of the most common mistakes that early R users make (we will see it again, applied to data frames, in ***Lesson 1.3: R Objects***). Notice what happens when we compare two integer vectors of the same length with `==`:

```{r}
2:4 == 1:3
```

You might expect two of these values to evaluate to `TRUE` -- but `==` compares values *by position*, not by set membership. To test whether values in one vector are found *anywhere* in another, use `%in%` instead:

```{r}
2:4 %in% 1:3
```
:::

::: now_you
{{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [True or false: Comparing two equal-length vectors with `==` tests set membership, so `2:4 == 1:3` returns `TRUE` wherever a value on the left also appears anywhere on the right.]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"}

`r torf(FALSE)`
:::

## Take-home points

Before you move on, here are the ideas from this lesson that are most worth holding onto:

* The **atomic vector** is R's fundamental object -- even a single number or word is a length-one atomic vector -- and every value in an atomic vector shares the same **type**. A vector's **class**, which affects how R treats the object, may differ from its underlying type.
* Unsuffixed numeric values have **double** type by default even when they are whole numbers; use `:` or an `L` suffix (like `1L`) when you actually want **integer**.
* When you need to preserve numeric values exactly, use `as.integer()` only on values that are already whole, because it **truncates** the fractional portion rather than rounding -- so `as.integer(2.8)` gives you 2, not 3.
* For characters, default to **double quotes** in this course; single quotes are only needed when the value itself contains a double quote (or you can **escape** that quote with a backslash), and `as.character()` will coerce any vector to character.
* A **factor** represents categorical values using integer codes and character levels, which is why its `typeof()` is integer; unless you say otherwise, its levels are **sorted** -- usually alphabetically according to the current locale -- rather than ordered by first appearance.
* Take control of a factor with the `levels` argument to set the order and the `labels` argument to rename the categories -- and remember `labels` are matched in the order of the `levels`, so setting labels without levels can mislabel a category.
* Logical `TRUE`/`FALSE` are coerced to 1 and 0 in numeric contexts, so you can `sum()` them to count `TRUE`s or take their `mean()` to get a proportion.
* Finally, `==` compares **by position** while `%in%` tests **set membership** -- so when you want to know whether values appear *anywhere* in another vector, reach for `%in%`, not `==`.
